name: Gareth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Gareth. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at Ashby Bakeries, the big bread plant off the bypass. I run the slicer and bagger at the end of line two, so loaves come out of the cooler, go through the blades, get bagged and clipped and go into crates for the lorries. Nine months in. I'm learning the oven side from a woman called Bev, who's been there since before the bypass was built.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the smell, still, even after nine months, and I like that it's calm compared to what I did before. I was a chef for twenty years, restaurants and a hotel, and kitchens are shouting and burns and Saturday nights. What wears me out is the slicer blades, they need changing and they will take your finger off, and sleeping in the day while my kids, Ellie and Josh, are fighting over the remote downstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it was mostly talk. In the canteen at three in the morning we'd have a laugh about it. I might post something cheeky in the five-a-side group chat, because a couple of the lads there were sure robots would be running everything by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can get on with learning the ovens. That's the better job, more pay, more skill, and it's the bit I like because it's closest to cooking. If nothing changes, I'd like to be running an oven by this time next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep working nights and ask for a fixed date to be signed off on the oven. He'd keep putting a bit of the night premium into savings each month. He'd probably finally book the holiday to Portugal they've talked about for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even. I've had enough big changes for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To scale recipes, mostly, when Sian's sister has a party and wants me to cook for forty. And once to sort out the five-a-side rota, which it did better than me. I don't use it at work, there's nothing to use it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you leave cooking, if you liked it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back and my family. Twenty years of standing over a stove at weekends meant I missed Ellie's first school play. When Sian went full time as a dental hygienist, one of us needed normal shifts, or at least shifts that weren't Saturday nights. The bakery pays better than the hotel ever did, which surprised me.

S0.say: Told you so, it was mostly talk, and we'd have a laugh about it in the canteen at three in the morning. I might post something cheeky in the five-a-side group chat for the lads who were sure robots would be running everything.
S0.think: It means I can get on with learning the ovens, which is the better job and the closest thing to cooking. If nothing changes, I'd like to be running an oven by this time next year.
S0.do: Keeps working nights at Ashby and asks for a fixed date for his oven sign-off. Puts part of the night premium into savings each month and books the long-delayed family holiday to Portugal.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, after enough big changes for a while.
S0.quote: I might post something cheeky in the five-a-side group chat, because a couple of the lads there were sure robots would be running everything by now.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is a former chef who left kitchens for family reasons and found the bakery calmer and better paid. He uses AI casually outside work and sees no use for it on the line. The oven is his goal because it connects to the craft he misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, the bakery's been automating for fifty years, this is just the next bit. Some jobs will go, some will come, you've got to be sensible about it. I wouldn't get angry about it in public, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the slicer and bagger is gone. It's already half automatic, and a camera could do my checking. The oven might hold out longer, because Bev does things by eye and feel that are hard to put in a computer, but I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd wait and see which jobs Ashby actually cuts and which it adds, then go for the one that looks safest once a couple of people have done it. He'd look at the maintenance apprenticeship the plant runs for adults, but only once he'd seen someone his age get through it. They'd keep saving and hold off on changing the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd keep an eye on it, like a pan you've left on low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go for the maintenance apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work. If a bloke like me, forty-odd, no qualifications past school, goes through it and comes out with a better job, I'm in. If it's all twenty-year-olds and computers, I'll stay where I am and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the oven might hold out. Is that hope or belief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Bev can tell if the dough's off by the way it moves on the belt, before any sensor says anything. I'd like to think that counts for something. But then I thought that about cooking too, and now half the hotel's food comes in a bag.

S1.say: Bakeries have been automating for fifty years and this is just the next bit, so you've got to be sensible about it. Some jobs will go and some will come, and getting angry in public is pointless.
S1.think: The slicer and bagger is gone, because it's already half automatic and a camera could do my checking. The oven might hold out longer, because Bev works by eye and feel, but I'm not sure.
S1.do: Waits to see which jobs Ashby cuts and adds, then goes for the safest one once others have tried it. Considers the plant's adult maintenance apprenticeship once someone his age gets through it, and keeps saving while holding off on a new car.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping an eye on it like a pan left on low.
S1.quote: Then I thought that about cooking too, and now half the hotel's food comes in a bag.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth treats change as normal and avoids blame, in keeping with his centre outlook. He needs proof from someone like himself before he'd retrain. He catches himself hoping that hand skill protects the oven job, then undercuts the hope with what he saw happen to hotel cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government and the companies to sit down quickly and agree a plan, because two years is no time. Support for people while they find their feet, and some honesty about what's coming. I'd say it, but I wouldn't be on the barricades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the bakery's finished for people, and so are the restaurants, give it a bit. But people will still want a birthday cake made by a person, or a proper Sunday roast from someone they know. That's my bet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd cut back to essentials and move a chunk of savings into an easy-access account so they can reach it. In the first months he'd start cooking for events at weekends, birthdays and wakes, through Sian's sister and word of mouth, to see if people will pay for food made by a person. He'd stay at Ashby as long as it lasted and not quit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be all right for money for a good while, but I'd be worried about what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, what you're for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been a cook or a baker my whole life. If a machine bakes better bread than Bev and cooks a better roast than me, what am I, a man who used to make food? Josh asked me once what my job is and I said I make the bread for the whole town. I like that answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the weekend cooking going now, not later, so I've got a name before everyone else has the same idea. Pay down a bit of the mortgage. And spend more time with the kids, honestly, because if work disappears I want them to remember me there, not asleep upstairs.

S2.say: We need the government and the companies to sit down quickly and agree a plan, because two years is no time. People need support while they find their feet, and honesty about what's coming, but I wouldn't be on the barricades.
S2.think: The bakery's finished for people and the restaurants won't be far behind. But people will still want a birthday cake or a Sunday roast made by someone they know, and that's my bet.
S2.do: Cuts back to essentials and moves savings into an easy-access account. Starts weekend event cooking through family and word of mouth in the first months, stays at Ashby to the end and pays down a bit of the mortgage.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about money, but about what he's for.
S2.quote: Josh asked me once what my job is and I said I make the bread for the whole town. I like that answer.
S2.fieldNote: With strong savings, Gareth's fear in the fast picture is about identity more than income. His steady nature gives way to an early move: starting weekend event cooking now to get a name first. He wants to spend more time awake with his children, which shows what night shifts have cost him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives everyone time to be sensible, so let's be sensible. Help people move into new work, and don't let the big firms walk away with all the gains. I'd say that at work and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to test my birthday cake idea properly. If it works by year two, I could build it up by 2031. If it doesn't, I'd still have the bakery wage and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd start weekend catering in the second year, after a year of watching whether people still want human-made food, and maybe do a food hygiene and small business course at the college. He'd stay at Ashby, learn the oven and keep saving. He'd look at a used catering van around year three if bookings are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a plan in it. That makes a big difference to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the fast one you'd start the cooking right away. Here you'd wait a year. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years there's no time to wait, you'd just have to jump. With five I can do what I normally do: watch for a bit, see if anyone else has made it work, then go. Sian says I'm like a cat at a door, I go out eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People paying properly, not just friends being nice. If the man who runs the café on the high street is still busy, and people are choosing him over the machine stuff, I'll know there's room. If his place closes, I'll think again.

S3.say: Five years gives everyone time to be sensible, so let's be sensible. Help people move into new work, and don't let the big firms walk away with all the gains.
S3.think: Five years is enough to test my birthday cake idea properly and build it up by 2031 if it works. If it doesn't, I'd still have the bakery wage and our savings.
S3.do: Watches for a year whether people still want food made by a person, then starts weekend catering in year two with a college hygiene and small business course. Stays at Ashby learning the oven and considers a used catering van around year three if bookings hold up.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but having a plan makes a big difference.
S3.quote: Sian says I'm like a cat at a door, I go out eventually.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Gareth go back to his natural rhythm: watch, check, then move. He uses a concrete test, the high street café, to judge whether human-made food has a future. His strong savings mean he can test an idea without risking the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no reason for a mess. Government, companies and workers should agree how it's going to go, step by step. I'd tell the lads at five-a-side to start thinking about it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage nearly gone, the kids grown up. I'd have time to build a small cake and catering business and see if it holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep working at Ashby for most of the decade and get signed off on the ovens. He'd grow the weekend catering slowly from around year two, invest in a catering van by year five, and go part-time at the bakery when the business covers it. They'd pay the mortgage off by about 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, mostly fine. It's a long way off and I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be nervous that the machines could make cakes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course. A robot can probably ice a cake better than me already. But I don't think people want a robot at their nan's ninetieth. They want me, with flour on my shirt, telling them the sponge is from her old recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Josh about work, with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something you can do with your hands and people, like cooking or nursing or Sian's job. And don't be scared of it, but don't trust anyone who says they know exactly what's coming, including me.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, so there's no reason for a mess. Government, companies and workers should agree how it goes step by step, and I'd tell the lads at five-a-side to start thinking now.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine: fifty-three, mortgage nearly gone, kids grown up. I'd have time to build a small cake and catering business and see if it holds.
S4.do: Stays at Ashby for most of the decade and gets signed off on the ovens. Grows weekend catering from year two, buys a catering van by year five, moves to part-time at the bakery when the business covers it and pays off the mortgage by about 2033.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, uneasy only at the edges.
S4.quote: But I don't think people want a robot at their nan's ninetieth.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Gareth build his human-made food idea at his own careful pace, with the bakery wage as backup. His bet rests on people wanting a person at family occasions, though he admits robots can already ice cakes. His advice to his children is honest about uncertainty, including his own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Money isn't the problem, we've been careful, but two years doesn't give me time to see if anything works before I have to jump. What would help is some kind of support for people setting up small businesses, help with the paperwork and a bit of money to start, and a straight answer from government about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd miss it. I would. Not the night shifts, but Bev, the smell, the lorries pulling out at five. You don't think a bread plant has a heart until you imagine it empty, with the machines just humming away and nobody to have a tea with.

headlineQuote: You don't think a bread plant has a heart until you imagine it empty, with the machines just humming away and nobody to have a tea with.
portrait: Gareth Rossi is 43, a former chef who has spent nine months on nights running the slicer and bagger at Ashby Bakeries while learning the ovens from Bev. He lives with Sian, a dental hygienist, and two children, with strong savings and a mortgage. He's pragmatic, avoids blame and likes to watch someone else try a thing before he does it. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and with AGI in five or ten years, when he'd slowly build a weekend cake and catering business, and anxious with two years, more about what he's for than about money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years wouldn't give him time to see if anything works before he had to jump.
whatWouldHelp: Support for people setting up small businesses, help with paperwork and some starting money, plus a straight answer from government about what's coming.
